David's Lament
DAY-vidz LAH-ment
noun phrase
David from Hebrew Dāwid (דוד), meaning “beloved” or “friend,” the name of Israel's second and greatest king, the man after God's own heart (1 Sam 13:14). Lament from Latin lamentum — a wailing, a mournful cry, from the root lam- possibly related to cry or weep; in Hebrew biblical poetry the lament form (qināh) is characterized by a falling 3+2 stress pattern, the meter of mourning, and by direct address to God in the language of complaint, petition, and renewed covenant trust.

See also: David's Lament

Biblical Definition

David's laments are among the most theologically daring literature in the entire canon — prayers that bring raw anguish, accusation, and confusion directly before the face of God without softening the complaint or abandoning covenant trust. Approximately one-third of the 150 Psalms follow the lament pattern; many are explicitly Davidic, including Psalm 22 (cited by Christ from the cross), Psalm 13, Psalm 55, and Psalm 88.

The lament form is not faithlessness but a specific form of faith: the sufferer addresses God directly (“My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” — Ps 22:1), voices the specific complaint (“How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?” — Ps 13:1), pleads for intervention, and typically moves through petition to renewed trust, even before circumstances have changed. The lament is thus the grammar of covenant prayer under trial: holding God to His promises while experiencing their apparent contradiction.

David's lamentation at the death of Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam 1:17) extends the form beyond personal suffering to national grief, demonstrating that lament encompasses the full range of human loss — relational, political, military, and theological. The conclusion of Psalm 55 models the lament's theological anchor: “Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.” (Ps 55:22) — the complaint does not end in despair but in covenantal casting of the weight upon the One who promised never to let the righteous fall.

The 1689 LBCF (21.3) confesses that prayer of all kinds — including confession and petition under suffering — is a duty required of all men, grounded in Christ's intercession. David's laments are the Old Testament school in which the church learns to pray honestly.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines lament as to mourn, to grieve, to express sorrow; and lamentation as the expression of sorrow, grief, or regret in cries and weeping. David's laments are the biblical tradition of holy complaint — prayers that bring suffering before God with full honesty while maintaining covenant faith.

LAMENT, v.t. [L. lamentor.] To mourn for; to bewail; to express grief for; specifically, to express grief by weeping and vocal complaint; applied in Scripture to public mourning for the dead (2 Sam 1:17) and to private prayer under affliction (Ps 13, 22, 55).

LAMENT, n. An expression of grief; a wail; in biblical poetry, the lament form (qināh) is a structured genre of prayer characterized by direct address to God, honest complaint about circumstances, petition for intervention, and frequently a turn toward renewed trust before the prayer's close.

David's laments constitute a school of honest prayer in the Psalter: Psalms 13, 22, 55, 88 and many others demonstrate that the Bible authorizes the full expression of grief, confusion, and apparent divine abandonment before God — not as rebellion but as the highest form of covenant prayer, which brings the complaint to the only One who can answer it.

Key Scripture

Ps 22:1 — "To the chief Musician upon Aijeleth Shahar, A Psalm of David. My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?"

Ps 13:1 — "To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?"

Ps 55:22 — "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved."

2 Sam 1:17 — "And David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan his son:"

Modern Corruption

Contemporary Christianity avoids lament in favor of relentless positivity — praise reports and victory language crowd out the biblical form of honest complaint; therapeutic spirituality reframes suffering as a personal growth opportunity rather than a covenant cry for divine intervention.

expand to see more

The contemporary evangelical worship culture has largely abandoned lament as a legitimate liturgical form. “Praise and worship” in the modern sense is almost entirely oriented toward celebration, thanksgiving, and affirmation — it has little room for the “How long, O LORD?” of Psalm 13 or the “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” of Psalm 22. This is not a minor liturgical preference but a theological impoverishment: the church that cannot lament has lost the ability to take suffering seriously in the presence of God, cannot pray honestly from pain, and tacitly suggests that genuine faith always feels victorious. The Psalter — the church's divinely authorized hymnbook — devotes more than a third of its pages to lament, and David's example models that lament is not faithlessness but faith's most rigorous expression.

A second corruption comes from therapeutic spirituality, which reinterprets suffering through the categories of personal growth and self-actualization. In the therapeutic frame, suffering is “an opportunity to develop resilience,” and the spiritualized version asks what God is “teaching you” through the pain — good questions, but they displace the lament's primary move, which is not self-reflection but God-address. David does not ask what God is teaching him in Psalm 22; he asks why God has forsaken him. The lament trusts that God can bear the full weight of human accusation and that covenant prayer requires honesty, not therapeutic management.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rooted in the Psalter's qināh poetic tradition and David's own covenant history of suffering, lament, and divine faithfulness; the form reaches its apex in Psalm 22, which Christ prayed from the cross, sanctifying every human lament as part of His redemptive suffering.

expand to see more

Hebrew qināh (קינה) — the funeral dirge or lament poem, characterized by a falling 3+2 stress pattern (the “limping” meter of mourning); the genre of 2 Samuel 1:17–27 and the book of Lamentations; structured by formal complaint, petition, and often a turn to trust or praise

Hebrew ’ānah (ענה) — to answer, to cry, to afflict; the root behind many lament verbs; in the Psalms God is consistently addressed as the One who both permits the affliction and is capable of answering it — the double tension that makes lament prayer possible

Ps 22 as the Christological lament — David's “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” is both his personal prayer in extremis and the prophetic script of Christ's cross-cry (Matt 27:46); Psalm 22 moves from abandonment (v. 1) through humiliation (vv. 6–8) to trust (vv. 9–10) to vindication and worldwide praise (vv. 27–31), the arc of all true lament

The imprecatory psalms (Ps 35, 58, 69, 109) — a subset of the lament tradition, where the complaint escalates to calls for divine justice against enemies; Reformed interpretation (Calvin, Spurgeon) reads these not as personal vengeance but as covenant cries for God's justice, legitimized by Christ who bore the full weight of imprecation in His own person

New covenant continuity of lament — Revelation's martyrs cry “And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?” (Rev 6:10), demonstrating that lament continues in the new covenant era and will not cease until the final judgment

Usage

"The regulative principle of worship (1689 LBCF 22.1) supports the use of the Psalms in corporate worship, and this means including lament psalms in the regular diet of congregational singing — Psalm 13, 22, 88, 137 — not only the psalms of triumph and praise."

"Walter Brueggemann's typology (from The Message of the Psalms) of Psalms as Orientation, Disorientation, and New Orientation provides a useful descriptive framework, though Reformed readers will insist that lament's “disorientation” is not a temporary spiritual crisis but a permanent form of faithful covenant address in an age of not-yet-consummation."

"The Christological reading of Psalm 22 — in which David's lament becomes the very words Christ cries from the cross — demonstrates that lament is not merely a human convention God tolerates; God the Son entered into the deepest lament possible, making David's prayer the vehicle of the world's redemption."
